turns.content: Good to see you. How has your mood been since we last spoke, and what would feel most helpful to focus on in our time together today?

Hi. Um, my mood has been pretty low, honestly. I've been thinking a lot about that expo loss still, and it's been hard to shake off. I guess I just want to figure out why I can't stop blaming myself for it, even when I know the whole team had an off day.

I really appreciate you naming that—it takes courage to sit with that kind of self-blame. When you notice yourself replaying the expo loss, what specific thought tends to come up first, almost like a reflex?

It's like, right away, I think "I'm just not good enough to compete." That's the first thing that pops into my head. I don't think about anyone else's mistakes or the pressure we were all under—it's just me, and how I let everyone down.

That's a heavy thought to carry, and I can hear how much it weighs on you. When that "I'm not good enough" thought shows up, what do you notice happening in your body or in what you feel like doing next?

I feel this knot in my stomach, kind of tight and cold. And then I just want to shut down, you know? Like, I'll put my controller down and walk away from any game or practice session because I already know I'm going to fail again.

That makes a lot of sense—your mind is connecting the thought to a physical feeling and then to an urge to pull back. And when you do walk away from practice, what tends to happen to that thought about not being good enough over the next few hours or days?

It actually gets worse, not better. I'll just sit there thinking about how I quit, and then I start telling myself that I'm not just a bad competitor, but that I'm lazy and weak too. It's like the thought just keeps snowballing until I feel completely useless.

It sounds like the very thing you do to protect yourself—stepping away—actually feeds the belief that you're not good enough. I'm wondering, if a teammate had the exact same off day at the expo and came to you with that same thought, what would you say to them?

I'd probably tell them that one bad day doesn't define them, and that everyone has off moments. I'd remind them of all the times they've practiced hard and done well. But for some reason, I can't seem to say those same things to myself. It's like I hold myself to a different, harsher standard.

That gap—between the kindness you'd show a teammate and the harshness you show yourself—is really important to notice. What do you think would happen if, the next time that "not good enough" thought pops up, you tried saying to yourself exactly what you'd say to that teammate?

It feels... weird to even think about. Like, I'd almost feel like I'm lying to myself, or making excuses. But I guess I could try it, just once, to see what happens. I'm scared it won't change anything, though—that I'll just hear my own voice and think, "Yeah, but you really did mess up."

That fear of it not working is completely understandable—it's a new skill, and it can feel awkward at first. Let's make it really concrete: what is the exact one-sentence version of what you'd say to that teammate, that you could try saying to yourself this week?

I'd say, "You're a skilled player, and one loss doesn't erase all the hard work you've put in." That's what I'd tell them. I guess I could try whispering that to myself next time the thought comes up, even if it feels fake at first.

That's a strong, clear sentence—and I love that you're willing to try it even with the discomfort. So between now and our next session, when that "I'm not good enough" thought arrives, your homework is to pause, take a breath, and say that exact line to yourself, either out loud or in your head. Then just notice what shifts, even a little. How does that plan feel to you?

It feels a little scary, but also kind of... hopeful? Like maybe I can break this cycle if I just give it a real shot. I'll try to do it, even if it's just once or twice before next time. Thanks for helping me see it that way.

That's a really honest and brave place to start—hopeful and scared can sit together. Before we wrap up, I'd love to know: how did it feel for you to talk through this today, and is there anything about our session you'd like to be different next time?

It actually felt good to get it out, to say all that stuff out loud. I usually keep it all bottled up, so just talking about it made me feel a little lighter. I think next time, maybe we could talk about how to handle that feeling of "lying to myself" when I try to be nicer, because that part still feels really uncomfortable.

I'm glad it felt lighter—that's a real step forward. And I think exploring that discomfort with self-kindness is an excellent focus for next time; it's a very common and important part of this work. So we'll pick up right there. Take care of yourself this week, and I'll look forward to hearing how it goes.
Good to see you. How has your mood been since we last spoke, and what feels most important to put on our agenda for today?

Hey. My mood's been pretty low, to be honest. I've been thinking a lot about my basketball team and that loss we took last week, and it's really getting me down. I guess what's most important is figuring out why I can't shake this feeling that we're doomed for the rest of the tournament.

I'm sorry to hear you've been feeling low—that loss clearly hit hard. So let's start there: when the thought "we're doomed" crosses your mind, what else goes through your head, and what do you notice happening in your body or in what you do next?

Well, when I think we're doomed, I start picturing us losing every single game from here on out. Like, it's not just one loss—it's like I can see the whole tournament going down the drain. My chest gets a little tight, and I just feel this heavy weight, like there's no point in even trying hard at practice. I end up just going through the motions instead of really pushing myself.

That tightness in your chest and the feeling of going through the motions—those are really telling. So the thought "we're doomed" leads you to picture total failure, which then drains the energy right out of your effort at practice. Can we look at that first step together—when you say "we're doomed," what's the actual evidence that one loss guarantees every future game will be lost?

I guess... there's not really solid evidence, is there? It's just that after that loss, it felt like all our momentum was gone. I mean, we've had good games before, but now it's like I can't remember any of them. All I can think about is how we messed up that one play, and then my mind just runs with it—like, if we can't win that game, how can we win any of the tougher ones?

It's really common for one vivid moment to blot out all the good memories—that's the mind trying to protect you, even if it's not helpful. So let's test it gently: can you think of a time earlier this season when your team lost a game, and then what actually happened in the very next match?

Yeah, actually... earlier this season we lost a close one to a team we should've beaten. I was pretty down after that too. But then we came back the next game and won by like ten points. We played better than we had in weeks. I'd kind of forgotten about that until you mentioned it.

That's a really helpful memory to have right now. So the evidence from this season actually shows that a loss doesn't predict doom—it was followed by one of your best performances. What might it mean for your practice today if you held that evidence in mind instead of the "we're doomed" picture?

Hmm... I think if I held onto that memory instead, I'd probably feel a lot more focused at practice. Maybe even a bit excited to see if we can bounce back like we did before. Instead of just going through the motions, I'd actually want to work harder and see what we're capable of. It's like a switch flips in my head when I remember that.

That shift from "going through the motions" to "I want to work harder" is exactly the kind of change that can make a real difference. So here's what I'm wondering: between now and our next session, would you be willing to try a small experiment—before practice each day, take just one minute to deliberately recall that bounce-back win and write down one piece of evidence that this team has recovered from losses before?

Yeah, I think I can do that. I mean, it's just a minute, and it's not like I have anything to lose by trying it. I'm a little skeptical, but I guess it's worth seeing if it actually changes how I feel before practice. I'll give it a shot.

That's a really open-minded attitude, and skepticism is totally fine—we're just testing it out, not committing to anything permanent. So to be clear, your homework is: before each practice this week, take one minute to recall that bounce-back win and jot down one piece of evidence of past recovery. How does that sound as a plan, and what's your sense of how today's session went for you?

That sounds like a solid plan. I think I can stick with it, even if it feels a little weird at first. As for today... I actually feel a bit lighter, you know? Like, I came in here feeling like everything was hopeless, and now I can see that's not the whole story. I'm curious to see how that little exercise goes. Thanks for helping me look at this differently.

I'm really glad to hear you feel lighter—that's a meaningful shift, and it came from your own ability to find the counter-evidence. I'm curious to hear how the experiment goes, and we'll check in on it next time. Take care of yourself between now and then, and I'll see you soon.
Good to see you. How have you been feeling since we last spoke, and what feels most important to put on the agenda for our time together today?

Hi. I've been alright, I guess. I went on a hike last weekend with some friends, and it just brought up all those old feelings again. I think I want to talk about why I can't seem to shake this idea that I'm a terrible hiker, no matter what I do.

I'm glad you got out with friends, and I can hear how frustrating it is that those old feelings showed up. So let's start there: when that thought "I'm a terrible hiker" popped into your head on the trail, what was happening right around that moment?

Well, we were on a trail that had a pretty steep, rocky section. Everyone else just seemed to handle it so easily, scrambling up without thinking about it. I was slower, and I had to stop a couple times to catch my breath. I just looked at them and thought, "See, you don't belong here. You're not like them."

That sounds like a tough moment—being slower while everyone else moves ahead can feel really isolating. When that thought "you don't belong here" came up, what did you feel in your body, and what did you do next?

I felt this tightness in my chest, and I kind of just stopped moving for a second. My face felt hot. I ended up just telling them to go on ahead without me, that I'd catch up later. I sat on a rock for a few minutes, just feeling stupid and disappointed in myself.

Thank you for sharing that. So there's a clear sequence here: you noticed you were slower, the thought "you don't belong here" appeared, your chest tightened, and then you chose to sit alone. I'm wondering—when you were on that rock, what evidence could you see that actually supports the idea that you're a terrible hiker, and what evidence might go against it?

The evidence for it... I mean, I was the slowest one. I had to stop. I couldn't keep up with people who actually know what they're doing. That's pretty solid proof, isn't it? But against it... I guess I did finish the hike. I made it to the top eventually, even if I was last. And I've done plenty of other hikes before that went fine. But it's hard to hold onto that when I feel so out of place.

It makes sense that the feeling of being out of place is so loud in that moment—it's a powerful emotion. But you've just named some real evidence on the other side: you finished the hike, you've done many before, and you made it to the top. If a close friend told you they were the slowest on a steep, rocky trail but still reached the summit, would you call them a terrible hiker, or would you see it differently?

No, I wouldn't call them a terrible hiker. I'd probably tell them that the steep, rocky parts are tough for everyone, and that finishing is what matters. Maybe I'd even say that being slower just means you're being careful or taking your time. But when it's me, it just feels different. It's like I have a separate set of rules for judging myself.

That's such an important insight—you have a different, harsher set of rules for yourself than you'd ever use for a friend. So let's try an experiment: if you were to apply your friend's standard to yourself, what would you say to that thought "you don't belong here" the next time you're on a trail?

I guess I'd say... "You do belong here. You're on the same trail, heading to the same place as everyone else. Being slower doesn't mean you don't deserve to be here." It sounds weird saying it out loud, like I'm trying to convince myself of something I don't fully believe yet. But I can see how that's more fair than what I usually tell myself.

That sounds like a really fair and kind counter-statement—and it's okay that it doesn't feel fully true yet; that often comes with practice. So here's a concrete idea for this week: before your next hike, could you write that sentence on a note and keep it in your pocket, and then read it to yourself the moment you notice that old thought creeping in?

Yeah, I could try that. It feels a little silly, but I guess it's worth a shot. I'll put it in my phone too, just in case I forget the note. The next hike I have planned is next Saturday, so I'll have a few days to get used to the idea.
That's a solid plan—having it on your phone as a backup is smart. Before we wrap up, how are you feeling about the session today, and is there anything you'd want to adjust or add for next time?

I'm feeling a bit better, actually. It helped to talk through that specific moment on the trail and realize I'm being harder on myself than I would be on anyone else. I think for next time, I'd like to check in and see if that note trick actually made a difference on the hike. That way I can figure out if it's just a nice idea or if it really helps.

I'm glad that felt helpful, and I think that's a great plan for next time—we'll look at what happened on the hike and whether that note shifted anything for you. Take care between now and Saturday, and I'll see you then.
Good to see you. How has your mood been since we last spoke, and what feels most important to put on our agenda today?

Hi. Honestly, my mood has been up and down. I still get really frustrated with myself when I notice I'm doing that thing where I write something off completely just because one small part of it isn't perfect. I guess what's most important today is figuring out why I can't seem to just enjoy things normally anymore.

Thank you for naming that so clearly. That frustration you feel toward yourself sounds exhausting, especially when it steals the enjoyment from things you'd otherwise like. Can you tell me about a specific moment this week when you noticed that all-or-nothing thinking creep in?

Yeah, it really is exhausting. There was this one moment yesterday—I was listening to a new rap album I'd been excited about for weeks. One track had a beat I didn't vibe with, and suddenly I just decided the whole album was trash. I literally stopped listening and felt this wave of disappointment. I couldn't even remember the songs I did like before that moment.

That's a really clear example, and I can hear how quickly that disappointment took over. So in that moment, the thought "this whole album is trash" came in, and it wiped out all memory of the songs you had enjoyed just minutes before. What feeling came up for you right after that thought landed?

I felt this heaviness in my chest, like a letdown. It was almost like I'd been tricked into getting my hopes up. And then there was this anger, not really at the artist, but at myself for not being able to just enjoy it like a normal person. It made me want to just shut everything off and not bother with music for a while.

That heaviness and anger toward yourself sounds really painful, and I can see how it would lead you to want to shut music out altogether. Let's look at that thought "I'm not able to enjoy things like a normal person" — what evidence do you have that other people never have moments where one part of something doesn't land for them?

I guess I don't really have any evidence. I mean, I see my friends hyping up albums even when they joke about skipping a track. But I always assumed they were just being polite or not as critical as me. When they say they love it, I think they mean they love every single second of it, not just most of it.

That's a really important distinction you've just made — the idea that "loving something" might mean loving the whole experience, not every single second of it. If we tested that assumption, what do you think your friend would say if you asked them whether they genuinely enjoy every single track on every album they love?

I think they'd probably laugh and say no. They'd probably tell me about tracks they skip or don't care for. I never really thought about it that way before. I just assumed everyone else was experiencing things perfectly, and I was the broken one for noticing the flaws. But maybe they just don't let the one bad part ruin the rest for them.

That's a really insightful shift you're making — noticing that the difference might not be that they experience things perfectly, but that they allow the good parts to coexist with the imperfect parts. How might it change how you listen to that album today if you gave yourself permission to hold both the track you didn't like and the ones you did, without letting one cancel out the other?

I think... I'd probably be able to finish the album. I might even find a few more songs I actually like. It's just hard to let go of that feeling that if it's not all good, then it's all bad. But I guess that's the part I need to work on—giving the good parts some space instead of smothering them with the bad.

That's a beautiful way to put it — giving the good parts some space instead of smothering them. Between now and our next session, I'd like to suggest a small experiment: pick one thing you usually enjoy, like an album or a movie, and when that all-or-nothing thought shows up, pause and deliberately name two specific things you did like before you decide whether to continue. How does that sound as a first step?

That actually sounds doable. I mean, it's not like I have to force myself to love everything—I just have to pause and notice the good parts before I trash the whole thing. I'll try it with a movie I've been hesitant to watch because I heard one bad review. I can probably name two things I like about it before making up my mind.

That sounds like a thoughtful and manageable experiment. Before we wrap up, I'd love to hear how today felt for you — was there anything that stood out or felt helpful, or anything you wish we'd touched on differently?

It felt... kind of eye-opening, actually. I think the part that stood out most was realizing my friends probably don't love everything perfectly either. I never really questioned that assumption before. I think just having that little experiment to try gives me something concrete to focus on instead of just spiraling. Thanks for listening.

I'm really glad that felt eye-opening, and I appreciate you sharing that honestly. That shift in perspective about your friends is a powerful one to hold onto. I look forward to hearing how your experiment with the movie goes, and we'll build from there next time. Take care until then.
Good to see you. How has your mood been since we last spoke, and is there anything in particular you'd like to make sure we cover today?

Hey, thanks. I've been... alright, I guess. A bit up and down. I think I'd like to talk more about how I compare myself to my friends. It's been on my mind a lot lately, especially after a dinner I had with some old college buddies last week.
Thanks for sharing that. It sounds like that dinner really stirred something up for you. Can you tell me a bit more about what was going through your mind during that evening with your friends?

Well, they were all talking about their promotions and bonuses, the kind of stuff you hear at these things. One guy's a manager at a big firm, another's in tech. And there I am, just a freelance accountant, you know? I felt like I had nothing worthwhile to contribute. I kept thinking, "They must think I'm a failure." I just sat there feeling smaller and smaller.

That sounds really tough—sitting there feeling like you didn't measure up. When that thought "They must think I'm a failure" came up, what did you notice happening in your body or in the way you acted?

I felt this tightness in my chest, like I couldn't really breathe deeply. I probably got quieter, just nodded along. I think I even made an excuse to leave a little early, said I had an early client meeting the next day. But really, I just wanted to get out of there. I didn't want them to see how uncomfortable I was.

It makes perfect sense that you'd want to escape that discomfort. So the thought "They must think I'm a failure" led to that tightness in your chest and then to leaving early. Now, I'm curious—what evidence do you have that your friends actually think you're a failure? Did any of them say something directly, or is that more of a guess you were making in the moment?

I mean, nobody said it out loud, no. But it's not like they'd say it to my face, right? People don't do that. It's more the way they talk about their own lives—the excitement, the clear path they're on. And then there's me, scraping by on freelance gigs. I guess I just assume they're thinking what I'm thinking about myself. Like, if I were in their shoes, I'd probably think I was a failure too.

That's a really honest and important observation—you're assuming they see you the same way you see yourself. Let's test that a little. When you picture one of those friends, say the one in tech, what do you actually know about his life outside of that one conversation? Does he ever mention struggles, doubts, or things he's not proud of?

Honestly, I don't really know. We don't talk that often outside of those group dinners. I guess he's mentioned being stressed about deadlines before, and once he said he felt like he was just a cog in a machine. But I never really paid much attention to that—I sort of glossed over it because it didn't fit my picture of him having it all together. I guess I just assume his problems are smaller than mine.

It's interesting that you noticed yourself glossing over his struggles. So there's evidence that he has his own difficulties, even if you tend to minimize them. What would it be like to hold both things at once—that he has a high-paying job and also feels like a cog in a machine—and still see your own path as just as valid?

I... I don't know. That feels hard to do. Like, on paper, his job looks way more impressive, right? But I guess if I really stop and think about it, he's not walking around happy all the time either. It's just tough to feel like what I do matters as much. I mean, I help people with their taxes and bookkeeping. It's not exactly glamorous or changing the world.

It sounds like you're comparing the outside of his life to the inside of yours, which is never a fair fight. Let me ask you this: when a client comes to you stressed about their taxes and you help them sort it out, what do you think that means to them in that moment?

I guess they're relieved, maybe even grateful. Some of them have told me I've saved them a lot of headache, or even money. I just never really let that sink in. I always think, "Well, anyone with a degree could do this," or "It's not like I'm curing a disease." So I downplay it. But... I mean, yeah, they do seem genuinely thankful. I just don't feel like that counts for much in the bigger picture.

It sounds like you have a habit of immediately dismissing your own wins. What if, just for this week, you tried a small experiment? Every time a client thanks you or you finish a task you handled well, I'd like you to pause for just five seconds and say to yourself, "That mattered to someone." No need to compare it to anything else—just let that sentence sit. Would you be willing to try that?

I guess I could give that a shot. It sounds a little silly, but I get what you're going for. Five seconds isn't that long, right? I'll try it. I just hope I don't forget to do it in the moment, because my brain usually jumps straight to the next thing I did wrong or what I still have left to do.

That's a really good point—your brain is used to fast-forwarding to the next worry. To help with that, how about we pair it with something you already do? For example, right after you close a client email or hang up a call, take that five-second pause before you open the next tab. Does that feel like a more concrete trigger you could remember?

Yeah, actually, that might work better. I always close an email and immediately start typing the next one. So if I just force myself to sit there for a moment after hitting send... I can picture that. I'll give it a real try this week. Can't promise I'll remember every time, but I'm willing to see what happens.
That sounds like a solid and realistic plan. Before we wrap up, I'd love to hear your honest take—what was the most useful part of our conversation today for you?

I think it was when you pointed out that I'm comparing my insides to everyone else's outsides. I never really thought of it that way. And that idea about actually noticing when I help someone, instead of just brushing it off—that stuck with me too. I guess I've been so focused on what I'm not, I forgot to see what I actually do.

I'm really glad that landed for you. That's a powerful shift in perspective, and it's something you can build on. So just to recap: this week, after you send a client email or finish a call, you'll take five seconds to acknowledge that what you did mattered to someone. And if you notice yourself comparing again, maybe you can gently remind yourself that you're only seeing the highlight reel of others' lives. I look forward to hearing how it goes. Take care of yourself until then.
Good to see you. How have you been feeling since we last spoke, and what feels most important to put on the agenda for today?

Hi. Honestly, I've been feeling pretty stuck since our last session. I think the most important thing for me today is to talk about this overwhelming fear that's been stopping me from even trying to start a new online business. Every time I think about it, I just feel like I'm going to fail again, so why bother?

I hear that feeling of being stuck, and it makes a lot of sense that you'd want to focus on that fear today. Before we dive in, could you tell me a little more about the last time that thought—"why bother, I'll just fail"—showed up? What were you doing right before it hit?

I was actually just scrolling through my laptop last night, looking at some potential product ideas I had bookmarked months ago. I got as far as opening one of the websites, and then that thought just crashed in. I closed the laptop and watched TV instead because it felt pointless.

So you went from curiosity and planning to shutting down completely in a matter of moments. When that thought crashed in, what emotion did you notice most strongly in your body—was it more of a heavy dread, or a tight, anxious feeling?

It was definitely a tight, anxious feeling—like my chest got all clenched up. It felt like a knot in my stomach too, like I was already bracing myself for the disappointment before I even tried anything.

That makes perfect sense—your body was already preparing for the worst outcome before you'd taken a single step. And it sounds like the behaviour of closing the laptop and turning on the TV gave you some immediate relief from that knot in your stomach. If we look at that pattern, what do you think that relief told your brain about the thought "I'm going to fail"?

I guess it told my brain that the thought was right, and that avoiding the whole thing was the safe move. Like, every time I close the laptop, I'm proving to myself that I can't handle it, so I just stop trying. It's like my brain learned that giving up feels better than risking that horrible knot in my stomach.

You've put your finger on exactly how that cycle works. So the short-term relief of watching TV is actually training your brain to believe that avoidance is the only way to feel safe. Now, I'm curious—when you look back at that moment on the sofa, what's the evidence that you truly "can't handle it," versus the evidence that you simply chose to avoid an uncomfortable feeling?

Well, when you put it that way... I guess the evidence that I can't handle it is pretty weak, actually. I mean, I handled the failures before—I got through them, even though they were hard. The only real evidence I have is that I chose not to sit with that awful feeling for a few minutes. But I've handled way harder things in the past, like dealing with the fallout from my last business closing down.

That's a really important distinction you've just made—you've already survived the very thing you're afraid of, and you came out the other side. If your best friend told you they were avoiding a new project because they were scared of failing again, and you knew they'd already handled a business closing down, what would you say to them about that knot in their stomach?

I'd tell them that feeling doesn't mean they're going to fail again—it just means they care enough to be nervous. I'd remind them that they're stronger than they think, and that avoiding it only makes the fear bigger in their head. Honestly, I'd probably tell them to just open the laptop and take one tiny step, even if they feel scared.

That's a really compassionate and wise thing to say to a friend. So if we take that same advice and apply it to you, what might one tiny step look like tonight—something so small that it feels almost silly, but that would break the cycle of closing the laptop and turning on the TV?

Maybe just... opening one of those bookmarked websites again, but not even committing to doing anything with it. Just look at the page for two minutes, close it, and then go do something else. That feels manageable—like I'm not forcing myself to make any big decisions, just proving I can look at it without the world ending.

That sounds like a perfectly sized experiment—small enough to feel doable, but powerful enough to test the prediction that looking at the page will be unbearable. How about we make it concrete: between now and our next session, you'll open one bookmarked site for two minutes, notice what happens to that knot in your stomach, and then you can choose to close it or stay a little longer. Does that feel like a fair homework step, and is there anything that might get in the way of trying it?

Yeah, I think I can do that. The only thing that might get in the way is if I let myself get too distracted before I even try, like if I start scrolling on my phone or turn on the TV first. But I think if I just go straight to my laptop when I get home from work, I can do it before my brain has time to talk me out of it.

That's a smart strategy—going straight to the laptop before your brain has a chance to argue with you. So the plan is clear: when you get home, you'll go directly to your laptop, open one site for two minutes, and then notice what happens. Before we wrap up, I'd love to hear how this session felt for you—was there anything that stood out or felt particularly useful today?

It actually felt really helpful. I think the biggest thing was realizing that I've already survived my worst fear, and that avoiding the feeling just makes it stronger. I never really thought about it like a cycle before—I just thought I was being realistic about my chances. So yeah, I feel a little bit lighter, like maybe I can actually try this tiny step and see what happens.

I'm really glad that landed for you—that shift from "being realistic" to seeing the cycle is a meaningful step. You've done good work today. I'll look forward to hearing how that two-minute experiment goes, and we can build on it from there. Take care until then.
Good to see you. How have you been feeling since we last spoke, and what feels most important to put on our agenda for today?

Hi, thanks for asking. I've been okay, I guess—still struggling a lot with this whole cooking thing, honestly. I think what's most important today is trying to figure out why I just can't seem to believe I'll ever be able to cook for myself, even though I really want to.
I appreciate you naming that so clearly. So when you think about cooking for yourself, what specific thought or image comes to mind first—what’s the very beginning of that struggle?

I picture myself standing in the kitchen with all these ingredients spread out, and I just feel completely lost. It's like my brain freezes and I think, "I don't know what I'm doing, and this is going to be a disaster."
That sounds really overwhelming—feeling frozen like that. When that thought, "this is going to be a disaster," shows up, what do you notice happening in your body or your mood right then?
My chest gets really tight, and I start feeling kind of shaky. My mood just drops—I feel stupid and hopeless, like why even bother trying if I'm just going to mess it up anyway.

It makes sense that your body would react that way when the thought feels so certain. If we looked at that thought like a detective for a moment—"this is going to be a disaster"—what evidence do you have from past experiences that supports that idea?

Well, every time I've tried to cook something simple, like pasta or eggs, it never turns out right. The pasta is either mushy or hard, and I always burn the eggs. And I watch those cooking videos online, but when I try to copy them, it just doesn't work. So that's my evidence—I've failed before, so why would this time be any different?
